---
title: "How I Check My Work"
subtitle: "The standard every project on this site is held to, and where my own work failed it."
toc: true
---

An analysis is only useful to a commander if it is right, and if the person briefing it
knows how it could be wrong. These are the checks I run before I call something a result.

## 1. Every number has a receipt

Each headline figure on this site traces to a script, a log, or a saved artifact in the
project's repository. If I cannot point to where a number came from, it does not appear.
Project pages show only results in that state.

## 2. Evaluate on data the model never saw

Performance is reported on held-out data, split the way the model will be used: by time
when the future is what matters, by unit or person when the model must generalize to new
ones. Training-time scores are diagnostics, not results.

## 3. Compare against something

A number without a baseline is not a finding. I report the naive alternative (the
majority class, last year's rate, a random policy, the current manual process) next to
the model.

## 4. Report uncertainty, not just the estimate

Win rates come with game counts and intervals. Model scores come with variation across
seeds or folds. Simulation outputs come with the number of replications behind them.

## 5. Don't test the hypothesis on the data that suggested it

Selecting variables and then testing them on the same data manufactures significance.
When a method selects, the inference happens on separate data, or with a correction
built for selection.

## 6. Say what the analysis cannot tell you

Every project page ends with its limitations: what the data does not cover, which
assumptions carry the result, and what would change the conclusion.

## Where I got it wrong

Applying these checks to my own finished work changed conclusions. I keep those
corrections visible, because catching them is the job.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Draft: confirm against the audit before publishing
The cases below are summarized from project notes and are being verified in the
portfolio audit. Remove this box once each is linked to its evidence.
:::

- **A 14-point gap between training and serving.** A maintenance-code classifier looked
  healthy in training. Re-measuring the model the way it is actually served exposed a
  pooling mismatch that silently cost 14 points of accuracy. *(WUC Predict)*
- **An effect size inflated by the experimental design.** A simulation study suggested
  melee armies win 73% of the time. The design picked one army list per faction, which
  confounded list with archetype. Later checks found the scenario inputs themselves were
  wrong (invented terrain, the wrong mission); re-run on the published terrain and mission
  cards, the melee advantage is smaller and still under test with list-level uncertainty.
  *(Rules-engine simulation)*
- **Measurement faults in an agent evaluation.** Three faults in how competition agents
  were scored invalidated much of the recorded evidence, which was re-classified rather
  than quietly kept. *(Card-game AI)*
